ref:benchmark.clickhouse.com.notes: An honest benchmark page. Provenance is shown, not claimed: '60 of 62' match bars, sources named for each field, an example answer with footnoted citations and monthly counts. The mono body text on a long line is slow to read, and the beige-on-beige panels are low in contrast. ref:instances.vantage.sh.notes: The densest, most directly useful figure table of the set: exact CoreMark scores, monospaced API names, filters on every column, region and price-unit controls right where you need them. ref:turbopuffer.com.notes: The best of the set at turning figures into the pitch. The dark-to-light bands, pixel-shadowed boxes and mono type are carried through with care. On phone it reflows well, though the limits table wraps awkwardly. A developer has no command or snippet on the home page.

ref:vercel.com.notes: Excellent type and restraint (the tight grotesk headline, the generous whitespace), but 'Agentic Infrastructure' with a triangle says little to a newcomer in ten seconds, and the page has almost no figures besides a customer stat. In this headless capture everything below the first section is blank (scroll-triggered content never appeared), so most of the page's length was empty: in practice it is a polished template with not enough said.

v1.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Make the pencil digits work, in every cell, desktop-light-00 and desktop-dark-top. The tails after the three ink places are set at about 8 px in low-contrast grey, so they can't be read. They have no right padding, so the long ones run into the column rule: row 02 c6i '3.883 593 521 982 312 7', row 06 every column ('0.858 435 309 448 242 2'), row 02 m5. Their grouping is irregular too: groups of three, then a stray single digit, and a different count per cell. Fix it at the source. Give each column a fixed tail width sized to the longest tail it holds, with padding before the rule. Set the tail in tabular figures one size step below the ink (not three) and at a contrast that passes, and group from the decimal point in threes so the stray digit always falls in the same place. The idea of exact digits with three places in ink is the best thing on the page, and at the moment it costs legibility.
2. Show which way is better, and help the eye compare across a row. GB/s (higher is better) sits next to ns, ms and µs (lower is better), and nothing says which way to read. Put a small 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' mark beside each unit (UNIT column, desktop-light-00; the unit at the right of each benchmark title on phone). Then add one quiet comparison cue per row: the best cell in ink-bold or underlined, or a hairline bar under each figure scaled to the row. Today a reader has to parse 70 long numbers to see that c8a wins memory and that m5 is 7× slower on syscall.
3. Show the spread and the count behind each figure. The Method keeps p5, p50 and p95, but the ledger shows only p50 and never how many Runs stand behind it. Under each median, add a one-line pencil row such as 'p5 12.49 · p95 12.51 · n 34'. Or put a single small range tick in the cell. This is what makes rows 10–14 meaningful: whether 131.284 against 131.094 is a difference or noise.
4. Say in the table itself when a row measures the volume or the service rather than the machine. Row 10 (all 131.1 MB/s, the gp3 baseline of 125 MiB/s), row 12 (all 333.3 µs, i.e. the 3,000 IOPS gp3 baseline), row 13 and row 14 are flat across machines. A newcomer will conclude that the machines are equal, or that the benchmark is broken. Add a short note in the NOTE column: 'Capped by the gp3 volume's 3,000 IOPS baseline; same on every machine.' Also fix row 12's description, 'How many direct reads … completes', when the figure is a time per completed read in µs. Either state it as time per read or also give the reads per second.
5. Phone, phone-light-04: the Machines table is clipped at the right edge. The processor names are cut ('Gran', '9R', '837') and the NETWORK and USD AN HOUR columns can't be seen at all, so on a phone the prices never appear. There is no scroll cue either. Make it a stacked card per machine, or two lines per row: type, vCPU and memory, then processor and price. On phone, also put each machine's price once in the per-benchmark tables, or in a sticky machine key, since the desktop header's prices are lost there.
6. Make the figures look like links if they are links. The intro says 'Each figure links to its Series' file', but no figure looks clickable in any screenshot. Give them a hover or underline treatment, or a small ↗ on the row. Showing a path to the evidence is the trust claim, so it should be visible.
7. Agents section (desktop-light-01, right half). The three curl commands and the URL list repeat the same three addresses. Keep the curl blocks, fold the schema URLs into a compact list, and add a short excerpt of a real Series response so a developer sees the shape (percentiles, n, method, evidence links) without fetching. Consider moving a one-line 'curl api.ledgermath.com/v1/index.json [COPY]' into the header meta block, which today has only a link. The section sits about two screens down.
8. Header meta (desktop-light-00, top right): the nanosecond timestamp '17:07:23.182448102 UTC' is honest but noisy where it appears first. Lead with something a person can read, such as 'Newest Run 2026-11-19 17:07 UTC, 52 min ago', and keep the full stamp in pencil or in 'How a figure is kept'. The phone version (phone-light-00) is a long block of text with no figure above the fold except the start of row 01; this would tighten it.

KEEP
The point of view: a 'book of record', ink and pencil, roman-numeral sections, double rules, Source Serif with Plex Mono for machine names. It is distinctive and carried through consistently, and nothing like a SaaS template. Also keep the one-sentence purpose paragraph at the top, the price in each machine column header, the cheapest-first column order, the NOTE column's definition of each repetition, the 'How a figure is kept' glossary with the kept, counted and failed counts, AWS's own price wording quoted, and the 70-of-187 selection rule stated under the table. The phone ledger, a small table per benchmark, is a real redesign, not a squeezed desktop. Dark mode keeps the character and reads well.

READS AS FALSE OR MISLEADING
Nothing looks invented, but four things will make a careful reader stop. (a) 'RUNS AT 04:10 · 10:10 · 16:10 · 22:10 UTC' next to a newest Run at 17:07:23 and an oldest at 23:36:41: say that a Run finishes some time after its boot, or the schedule looks wrong. (b) 'FAILED, KEPT 0' out of 6,335 looks too clean without context. If it is true, the italic definition beneath it helps; consider linking to where a failure would be shown. (c) The 'how many' wording in row 12 against a figure in µs (see 4). (d) The flat disk and S3 rows shown without explanation can read as a defect in the measurement.

v2.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Put the spread on the page, not behind hover. DATA says 'hover for p5 and p95' (desktop-light-00, the paragraph above the table). Hover doesn't exist on a phone, doesn't show in a screenshot, and is invisible to a reader skimming. For a project whose whole case is exact, honest numbers, showing p50 alone hides the one thing that tells you whether two machines really differ (e.g. syscall 93.241… vs 93.242… on i4i and c6i, or GET-from-S3 22.59 vs 22.93). Add a small p5–p95 line or a faint range tick under each figure, at the same weight as the n= line.
2. Phone rows drop the provenance. On phone-light-01 to -03 each benchmark shows machine plus figure only: the n= count and the Series link (the hash) that desktop prints under every figure are gone. STATUS still promises 'linked from each figure'. Put n (and the range from change 1) on phone as a third, dim column or a second line. It costs little height and keeps the page's main promise on every screen size.
3. Say what the disk rows actually measure. 'Read a file sequentially' is 131.0–131.3 MB/s on all five machines, and 'Random 4 KiB, 64 in flight' is 333.3 µs everywhere (desktop-light-01, the DISK group). Those numbers are the gp3 volume's provisioned limits (125 MiB/s, 3,000 IOPS), not anything about the machines. An agent estimating a cost from this page will wrongly read them as machine properties. Add a one-line note on each affected row (or on the DISK heading) saying the figure is the volume's cap. Treating the cause beats leaving five identical numbers to explain themselves.
4. Help comparison across a row. Each row shows five 17-digit strings and no direction. Add 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' next to the unit (the rust GB/s and µs at the left), and mark the best figure in each row with a subtle mark (weight or an underline, not a colour flood). Comparing machines is the main job of this table, and today the reader has to work out direction from the unit.
5. Get a figure above the fold. On desktop-light-00 the first 900 px end at the machine header row, so a newcomer sees no measured number on the first screen. Shorten the paragraph under SYNOPSIS (it repeats what FILES says), or pull the first benchmark group up beside SYNOPSIS, so that at least one row of real figures shows on the first screen. The page's claim is 'measured figures'; show one immediately.
6. Fix the copy that contradicts the units. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads … completes' but the unit is µs per read. 'Sort 1 MiB' and the memory rows say 'How fast' over a time unit. 'Lock and unlock a mutex' repeats '(10,000 critical sections)', and its µs-per-10,000 forces mental division; consider saying ns per lock/unlock pair, or saying so plainly. In MACHINES the network column mixes 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit'; normalise it, or label it as AWS's own wording.
7. Stronger landmarks in the long table. The group headings ('## MEMORY', '## COMPUTE' …) are small rust caps, about the same size as the row text. The three description lines per row (description, italic 'one repetition', italic 'setting') are small, grey and long, so on desktop the 14 rows blur together. Give the groups more space and weight, and consider putting 'one repetition / setting' on a single line in a lighter, collapsible register. The 'p50' label sits alone at the left of the machine-header row; move it to head the unit column, where it means something.
8. The series hash under each figure (a0faf4326dd7, etc.) reads as noise to a person. Either make the figure itself the link and drop the hash, or prefix it with something readable ('series ↗', 'evidence'), so its purpose is clear without reading the DATA intro.

STRONG — KEEP
- The man-page concept (LEDGERMATH(5), NAME/SYNOPSIS/DESCRIPTION/EXIT STATUS/FILES/SEE ALSO) suits a project that publishes a file format for developers and agents, and it is carried through with real discipline, header to footer. It is distinctive and not a template.
- STATUS: newest and oldest Run to the nanosecond, kept/counted/failed, schedule, zone, price copy time. This is the best freshness-and-provenance block of any page in the comparison set.
- SYNOPSIS: three real curl lines with comments and copy buttons, plus FILES and schemas in SEE ALSO. The way in for an agent is obvious within seconds.
- Exact figures that are decimal-aligned, with the first four significant digits bright and the rest dim. This keeps the no-rounding promise while staying scannable. The per-row 'one repetition' and 'setting' definitions are excellent.
- METHODS in plain text with the R type 7 formula and the 'counted' rule, and EXIT STATUS '0 Runs failed of 6,335': trust you can audit.
- The phone version is designed, not squeezed. Per-benchmark machine lists with aligned decimals, and machine cards in place of the wide table.
- Dark mode: the amber accent on near-black is well judged, and the hierarchy holds.

READS AS FALSE OR MISLEADING
- On phone, 'hover for p5 and p95' and 'linked from each figure' promise things the phone layout doesn't visibly give.
- The identical disk figures, with no note, invite the false reading that all five machines have the same storage performance (see change 3). i4i.2xlarge even lists a local 1875 GB NVMe in MACHINES, which makes the 131 MB/s look like that machine's disk speed when it is the EBS root volume's.
- 'How many … completes' over a µs unit (the Random 4 KiB row) states the wrong kind of quantity.

v3.notes:
CHANGES, most valuable first
1. Get figures onto the first screen. On desktop-light-00 the top 900 px holds the title, timestamps, the abstract and the Data availability box; the first number (Table 1) starts around y=1790, after an Introduction that mostly repeats the abstract. Fold the Introduction's three points (i-iii) into the abstract or a short line under it, move Methods (section 4) below Access (section 5), and start Table 1 directly under the abstract/Data availability block. A benchmark home page should show a benchmark above the fold; vantage and ClickBench show data straight away.
2. Make Table 1 a matrix you can scan in one view. Right now each of the 14 rows carries a two-line description, so the 14x5 table runs to about 1.3 desktop screens and you can't compare one machine across benchmarks without scrolling. Drop the descriptions to one short line in smaller type (or move them into the Figure 1 captions, where they already partly sit). Align numbers on the decimal point, not the right edge: '3297 / 1689 / 858.4' and '26.39 / 6.851' are hard to compare as set. Add a direction cue for each unit (higher is better for GB/s and MB/s, lower for ns, µs and ms). Style the cells so they look like links, since the caption says each one links to its Series file but nothing shows it.
3. Settle the rounding contradiction. The project's stance is that figures are exact, and section 4.3 says 'This page changes only units, by moving the decimal point', with note 3 adding 'Nothing on this page is ... computed from the figures'. But Table 1 and Figure 1 round to four significant digits. Either show the exact p50 in the main table (Table S1 shows that digits grouped in threes, in mono, read well) or rewrite 4.3 and note 3 to say that Table 1 is rounded for reading and S1 is exact. As it stands, the page's own words are false about the page.
4. Rethink Figure 1 (desktop-light-01 to -02, about two screens). Zero-based linear scales are honest, but at this zoom most p5-p95 bars shrink to slivers. For a general reader the panels mostly redraw the medians already in Table 1, and the pale pink bars (light) and brown bars (dark) are low-contrast on top of that. Either merge spread into Table 1 (p5-p95 as a small inline bar or as numbers next to each median, so the medians aren't printed twice) or keep the panels but make them smaller, with darker spread bars and the count of Runs (n) beside each row. n is now visible only in Table S1.
5. Phone (phone-light-01 to -08, about 15,000 CSS px): much of the length comes from duplication. Each median appears in Table 1's per-benchmark lists and again in Figure 1. Choose one. The section 5 code block (phone-light-07) clips every curl URL at the right edge ('…/v1/index.', '…/v1/series'), which breaks the one thing a developer wants to copy: wrap the URLs or break them after '/v1/'. The Table 2 cards on phone are good; give Table 1 something equally deliberate, such as a compact per-machine toggle, rather than 14 stacked lists.
6. Show what you get. Section 5 and the Data availability box list addresses and schemas but never show a few lines of the JSON: one figure with its Method, version, n and Series id. An agent developer decides from that excerpt. Put one under the first curl.
7. Trim academic props that carry no information. 'Keywords', the envelope 'Correspondence:' that points to a JSON file (it reads as a contact address), the vertical arXiv-style stamp in the left margin, and nanosecond timestamps in the hero (keep them in Notes; show the hero to the minute) all add noise. Use the space to say who the page is for in the title deck. The phrase 'for agents and developers' is now buried in the sidebar and in the last sentence of the abstract.
8. Fix the benchmark descriptions that disagree with their units. 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' says 'How many direct reads … completes', but the figure is µs per completed read. Check every row's description against its unit, in Table 1 and in the Figure 1 subtitles.

KEEP
The scientific-report concept, carried through with real care: numbered sections, footnotes, equations (1)-(3), a reference list that points into the API, and the supplementary table. It fits a project whose whole claim is 'a source for each number'. Keep the Data availability box with a copyable curl on the first screen, plus the First Run, Latest Run and Prices copied stamps and '6,335 counted, 0 failed'. Table S1 is excellent: every digit grouped in threes, n per Series, and a linked Series id per row; it is the best exact-figures presentation I've seen in this set. Keep Table 2 printing AWS's price and description verbatim, the quoted 'which Runs count' rule in section 4.5, the restrained cream-and-oxblood palette with a warm, legible dark mode, the STIX/Plex pairing with machine names in mono, and the phone card layout for Table 2.

FALSE OR MISLEADING
- Section 4.3 and note 3 claim the page only moves decimal points and computes nothing, yet Table 1 and Figure 1 round to four significant digits. Table 2's 'cheapest first' is also an ordering the page imposes.
- The 'Random 4 KiB reads' description ('how many reads') doesn't match its unit (µs).
- 'Correspondence: api.ledgermath.com/v1/index.json' with an envelope icon implies a contact channel; it is a data file.
- Nothing visible marks Table 1's figures as links, though the caption says each one links to its Series file.
- The disk rows (131.1 MB/s, 333.3 µs) are the same on every machine, probably because of the gp3 volume's provisioned limits. Footnote b names the gp3 root volume, but a reader comparing machines may still read those rows as machine performance. A one-line note would prevent that without interpreting the data.

v4.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Help the reader compare, which the board does not do yet. In desktop-light-00/01 every cell is the same black number. Nothing marks the best or worst machine in a row, there are no bars, and nothing says whether higher or lower is better beyond the small 'MEDIAN RATE/TIME' label. Mark the best value in each row (a yellow underline or a filled chip in the house style), and put a short 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' next to MEDIAN RATE/TIME. A thin in-cell bar scaled to the row would also work. Right now a reader has to do the comparison in their head 70 times.
2. Use one unit across each row. In CPU 06 (Sort 1 MiB), c8a.2xlarge shows '858.4 µs' between '3.297 ms', '1.689 ms' and '2.830 ms'. When you scan the row, 858.4 looks like the biggest number when it is actually the fastest. Pick the unit per benchmark (0.8584 ms), not per cell. The exact line underneath can keep every digit.
3. Show the spread. The section intro says each figure is a p50, and section 04 defines 5th/50th/95th percentiles, but the board shows no range anywhere. For a benchmark site, how noisy a figure is matters as much as the figure itself. Add p5–p95 in small type under the exact line, or as a whisker on the bar from change 1. It is the strongest trust signal this data has, and the page leaves it out.
4. Make the board half as tall. Each row is 150–210 px because the description, the 'One repetition' line and the config line all sit in the left column, while the five figure cells use only their top third and leave large empty white blocks (desktop-light-01, OS 08 and DSK 12 especially). Keep the title and one line of description in the row and move 'One repetition' and the config into a hover/expand or a footnote. The whole 14×5 board should fit in about 1.5 desktop screens, so a visitor can see all of it.
5. Explain the disk rows, or they will mislead. DSK 10 reads about 131.1 MB/s on every machine, which is 125 MiB/s, the gp3 default throughput. DSK 12 reads 333.3 µs everywhere, which is exactly 1/3000 s, the gp3 default IOPS. These rows measure the EBS volume's provisioned limits, not the machines. The page says 'root EBS gp3 volume' in the description, but a reader comparing machines will conclude 'disks are identical'. Add one sentence on the Disk band (for example 'every machine boots the same default gp3 root volume: 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, so these rows show the volume's limits'). It will make the project look sharper, not weaker.
6. Rethink the hero. On desktop the left half's h1 is the wordmark 'LEDGERMATH', which repeats the logo in the bar above it. The right half is a large flip clock that says one thing: newest Run 17:07. Make the h1 a statement ('Measured AWS server benchmarks, every Run kept') and shrink the clock into a strip, which frees room for a glimpse of real figures or a JSON response above the fold. On the phone (phone-light-00) the clock comes BEFORE the name and the explanation, so the first thing a phone visitor sees is a decorative clock with no context. Move it below the intro there.
7. Show what an agent gets back. Section 03 has the curl commands and the schema table, which is good, but no response. Add a short excerpt of index.json, or of one Series file, showing a figure with its Series address, so 'cite every figure' becomes something you can see. Also make the cells look like links (the intro says each figure links to its Series file, but nothing in a cell shows that), and show one Series URL on hover/focus.
8. Phone details. The board turns into 14 cards × 5 machine rows, about nine phone screens. Consider a sticky machine/benchmark switcher or collapsing each category. The shell block wraps URLs mid-path ('…/v1/' then 'index.json'), and the schema table breaks 'series-/list' and '<yyyy-mm-/dd>.json' (phone-light-06). Give the file column the width, or let the block scroll sideways.

KEEP
- The house style: yellow/black/cream, condensed uppercase display type, a monospace data voice, numbered sections. It feels like a ledger or a departures board, and it holds together in light and in dark. The dark mode (desktop-dark-*) is genuinely well done, not just inverted.
- The cell's structure: a large figure, the exact value with every digit underneath, the newest-Run time and the Run count. This is the right information in the right order.
- Machine column headers that carry vCPU, memory and $/h, ordered cheapest first. The machine cards that quote AWS's own price-list wording ('$0.096 per On Demand Linux m5.large Instance Hour') plus the dated price file link: excellent provenance.
- The category bands with coded IDs (MEM 01, CPU 05…) and colour rails.
- The Method printed verbatim, the 'failed Runs are kept and shown, never dropped' line, and Failed Runs 0 shown up top.
- On the phone, the board as a card per benchmark, with machines as right-aligned rows, is a real redesign, not a squeezed table.

READS AS FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- DSK 12's description says 'How many direct reads the gp3 volume completes…' (a rate), but the figure is a MEDIAN TIME in µs per read. The wording and the number disagree.
- The board intro says 'The large figure is rounded', and then the Method block ends with the quote 'Every number is exactly as the Methods' Derivations hold it.' Both can be true, but side by side they jar for a project that 'does not round'. Say that the exact value is the figure and the large one is a display aid.
- 'SERIES 187' in the hero stats, while the board shows 70 cells. That is unexplained jargon on the first screen, and the mismatch makes the reader wonder what is missing. Either explain it (groups and variants) or show the count that matches what is on the page.
- The disk rows that are identical across machines (see change 5) will be read as a machine finding when they are a volume setting.
- Two self-quotes styled as pull-quotes ('Version 1 only ever gains fields…' attributed to 'THE API, ON VERSIONING', and the closing quote with no attribution) read like invented testimonials. State them plainly instead.

v5.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Fix the hero figure's digit tail (desktop-light-00, phone-light-00). The red '2615200030773' next to the giant 12.50 reads as a separate 13-digit number, like an ID, not as the rest of 12.502615200030773. On the phone it ends up bottom-left, cut off from the 12.50 by white space, with GB/s on the right, which is worse. Make it look like a continuation: keep it on the same baseline as the '12.50', start it with a hairline or the leading '…', set it smaller and lighter, or print the full value once underneath as the table does. The page's whole claim is exact figures, so its headline number has to be readable without effort.
2. Give the hero figure a reason, or pick a figure that has one. 'm5.large reads memory at 12.50 GB/s' is the cheapest machine's least surprising number. A newcomer gets no comparison and no reason to care. The What/Where/From/Source strip is excellent, so keep it, but either pick a figure that shows what LedgerMath is for (a spread across the five machines, or a cost-per-unit figure built from the price file) or add one line of comparison beside it, e.g. the same benchmark on the other four machines as small numbers.
3. Make the table comparable, not just readable (desktop-light-00/01). The figures are left-aligned and set ragged: 0.8584 next to 3.297, 101.2 next to 76.68. Right-align or decimal-align each column with tabular figures. Mark each row 'higher is better' or 'lower is better' (rows switch between GB/s rates and ns/µs/ms times, and nothing says which way is good). Consider a quiet mark on the best cell in each row. At the moment a reader has to do every comparison in their head.
4. Show spread and Run count per cell, not only in the hero. Only the hero says '36 counted Runs'. Every other cell is a bare p50 with no count and no p10/p90 or range. That matters most where cells are nearly equal (Hash 101.2 vs 101.2, syscall 93.24 vs 93.24, the disk rows). A small 'n=36 · p10–p90' line under the full-precision digits would carry the 'judge afterwards' message into the table itself. Today the table only asserts.
5. Explain the disk rows as limits of the volume (desktop-light-01 'Disk'). Read a file sequentially is 131.1 MB/s on every machine, and Random 4 KiB, 64 in flight is 333.3 µs on every machine. Those are the root gp3 volume's default throughput and IOPS caps, not a property of the machine types. Without a one-line note at the group heading, an agent or developer will read them as 'all five machines have equal disks'. Also, 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads … completes' but the figure is a time per completed read in µs. Make the description match the figure.
6. Cut the phone page's length by redesigning the table, not by stacking it (phone-light-00 to -05). Five full-width machine rows for each of 14 benchmarks makes about 10,000 px of identical blocks, and benchmarks can't be compared with each other. Use a compact 5-row grid with short machine labels, a sticky machine-name column, or one horizontally scrollable table with a pinned first column. Collapse the grey 'Median time of one repetition…' paragraph behind a disclosure. The per-benchmark card is clean, but the page's length isn't justified by what it shows.
7. Tighten section 02's stat strip (desktop-light-02). The five columns break the four-column grid used everywhere else. '10 November' and '19 November' wrap onto two cramped lines at display size while '17:07', '6,335' and '187' sit on one. Use one date format at one size (e.g. '10 Nov') or go back to four columns. The nanosecond timestamps under them are a nice touch, so keep them.
8. Agents section and hero curl (desktop-light-00 top right, desktop-light-02). The hero curl block breaks 'curl' onto its own line, so it doesn't look like one copyable command. Widen it or shorten the line, and add a copy button to every command block. Show what comes back: a 6–10 line excerpt of index.json or one series entry with its percentiles and Run links would answer 'what do I get' faster than the prose does. The Machines section (04) repeats the price row from the table header at display size; it could be half as tall.

WHAT IS STRONG AND MUST BE KEPT
- A clear point of view: Swiss/International-style grotesque, tight display headlines, one red accent used only for the hero figure and its matching table cell. It doesn't look like a template, and the restraint carries through in dark mode.
- The headline 'AWS machines, measured four times a day.' with the boot times in the header bar: the newcomer knows in seconds what this is and how fresh it is.
- The What / Where / From / Source strip under the hero: provenance attached to a figure, in four short cells.
- Big four-digit figure with every digit underneath, with units set small: the right answer to 'exact but scannable'.
- The Run → Series → Method → Figure glossary, and quoting AWS's own price string under each machine ("$0.096 per On Demand Linux m5.large Instance Hour"). That is provenance done well.
- Three labelled curl commands, the schema list and the 'Version 1 only ever gains fields' promise.

ANYTHING FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- The hero's digit tail reads as an unrelated number (see 1).
- The disk rows invite a wrong conclusion about the machines (see 5), and the '64 in flight' description says 'how many' over a time figure.
- Small consistency check: the stat strip says the oldest Run is 10 November 23:36, while the hero's Series runs '11 November to 19 November'. That may be correct (different Series), but a reader will notice it. Saying which Series starts when, or labelling the window as 'counted Runs', would head this off.
- The intro says 'every figure links to its Series file', but nothing in the table cells looks like a link (no underline, no hover cue visible). Either show that they are links or soften the claim.

Every cell is right-aligned on its last digit, so with 13 to 17 significant digits the decimal points wander and 3296.71… sits visually level with 1688.80… only by accident. Align each column on the decimal point (tabular figures, pad the fraction), and set the digits after the fourth significant one in a lighter weight or with thin-space grouping in threes. In rows 09/10/11 and 12/13/14 the plot areas start at three different heights because the ZOOMED note and overview sit in only some cards, leaving dead gaps under the short descriptions (11 'Read 8 KiB from disk', 13 'Write 8 KiB durably', 07 'Make a system call'). The 'Every digit' heading and the 'How a figure is made' cards are fine, but the 'counted' paragraph in 'Method series v1, in the API's own words' is a single 80-word sentence: break it into a short list.

STRONG, keep:
- The instrument itself: median dot plus p5–p95 whisker, five machines in a fixed price order, a shared zero-based scale, value printed in a right column, 'more/less is faster' in each header. It is honest and scannable, and it reads as LedgerMath's own visual language.
- The ZOOMED treatment, with a 'from 0' overview strip that shows where the zoomed box sits and a break mark on the axis. This is the best handling of non-zero scales I have seen on a page like this; keep it exactly.
- The hero 'How to read an instrument' chart with inline p5/p95 labels and a three-line legend. It teaches the grammar before the grid.
- The stat strip (newest Run to the nanosecond, 6,335 kept / 0 failed, 187 Series, oldest Run, prices copied) and the footer that repeats the snapshot time.
- The dark API section: endpoints with comments, a real series.json row whose p50 (19581876183.05 B/s) matches the 19.58 GB/s in the chart, and the four-cell 'what you get' grid. Also the boot clock and the Method quoted in the API's own words.
- A restrained palette with one accent, monospace for machine names and figures, and a dark mode that has been designed rather than inverted.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED:
- 'hover any figure for every digit' on a touch phone is untrue there.
- Four-significant-digit rounding in the cards sits uneasily with the project's no-rounding stance. It is disclosed, but the hero chart's printed values are rounded with no marker on the figures themselves.
- 'each one links … to its evidence': the page never shows a Run's evidence, only Series files.
- Card 12's description describes a count while the chart shows a time.
Nothing else looked invented: the figures, Run counts, prices and JSON sample agree with each other wherever I could cross-check them.

Collapse the mono 'Median time of one repetition…' line behind a tap, or tighten the row height. On phone, the full-digit line sits to the left of the rounded figure, the reverse of desktop. Put it under the figure, as desktop does, so the two layouts read alike and the line can be shorter.
7. Settle on one display voice. The H1 is a bold grotesque, while every other heading (The same numbers, Point your agent here, The Methods) and the Q are a high-contrast serif. The top of the page looks as if it came from a different template than the rest. Set the H1 in the serif as well, or demote the serif.
8. The small grey mono metadata under each benchmark and the field paths in the answer table are about 10–11 px, light grey on cream. They are hard to read in light mode and only just legible in dark. Raise their size or contrast one step. Rename the 'Copy first line' button to say what it copies (for example 'Copy index URL'), or give each curl its own copy button.

KEEP
- The worked Q&A with numbered sources, and 'Every figure in the answer, as the files hold it' with the exact JSON field path, rate code and raw pricePerUnit string. This is the best provenance device I have seen for this kind of site. It shows, rather than claims, that every number has a source.
- The agent's restraint line ('I haven't compared machines or worked out a cost per sort'). It is honest and on-brand.
- The rounded large figure with the full-digit line beneath. It answers 'exact' and 'scannable' at once.
- The cited cell highlighted in the table, with the 'priced in the answer above' tie-in on the machine card. These threads connect the page.
- 'Point your agent here': curl lines, a ready-to-paste prompt and schema links. It is concrete and usable.
- The boot timeline and the Runs/Series/oldest/newest/prices-copied strip. It shows freshness without clutter.
- Warm paper with a rust accent, and a dark mode that holds up. Category labels (MEMORY, COMPUTE …) give the table rhythm.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- The Random 4 KiB description describes a rate while the figure is a time (see 4).
- Identical disk/S3 figures across machines, left unexplained, invite the false conclusion that the machines perform the same on I/O (see 3).
- 'The large figure is rounded to four digits' is stated openly, and every digit sits beneath it, so it is not misleading. The rounded figure is visually dominant, though, on a project that says it does not round. Keep the full digits as prominent as they are now, or more.
- No invented figures spotted: the Run counts (34 for one Series, 6,335 across 187 Series), the dates and the prices agree with each other across the sections.

v8.notes:
CHANGES, MOST VALUABLE FIRST
1. Stop rounding the headline table by default (desktop-light-01, the line above the table: 'Rounded to four significant figures… Every digit' toggle off). The project's stance is exact figures, the hero card shows every digit, the JSON caption says 'nothing rounded', and the section is headed 'as measured'. Yet the main table, the thing most people compare, shows rounded values. Show the exact p50 by default in tabular mono, with digits past the fourth significant figure in a lighter tone if density is the worry. Then remove the toggle or flip it to 'Short form'. This fixes the page's one real contradiction at its cause.
2. Show the spread and the Run count in the table itself, not only on hover (desktop-light-01/02, every figure cell). Each cell already carries a dotted underline. Draw a thin p5–p95 whisker there, the same mark as the hero card's range bar, and add 'n=36' in the row's unit line or the column header. On phone, 'Hover a figure' does nothing (phone-light-03). Right now the table carries no sign of variance, so the trust story stops at the hero card.
3. Make the table denser and easier to compare. Rows are about 95–115 px tall on desktop because each one repeats a two-line description and a unit line. Fourteen rows take up most of two screens, and you cannot see Memory and Disk together. Put each description in a tooltip or in a single line in a lighter tone. Keep the unit and 'less/more is faster' as a small column. Mark the best figure in each row (bold or a rust dot) so the eye can scan for winners. Instances.vantage.sh shows how dense a figure table can get and still read well.
4. Say why the Disk figures are identical across all five machines (desktop-light-02, Disk group: 131.1 MB/s ×5, 333.3 µs ×5, ~900 µs ×5). These are the root EBS gp3 volume's baseline limits (125 MiB/s, 3,000 IOPS), not properties of the machines. i4i.2xlarge's local 1×1875 NVMe SSD, listed in its machine card, is never measured. Add a one-line group note ('all five read the same gp3 root volume, so these figures are its limits'). Without it, a reader or an agent will take these as machine comparisons.
5. On phone, the three curl commands look identical (phone-light-06, For agents section). Each one is cut to '$ curl https://api.ledgermath.com', so you cannot tell index, series and prices apart. On desktop the prices URL also runs under the Copy button (desktop-light-03). Wrap the command, or show the path first ('/v1/index.json', with the host in the label). Never truncate the part that tells the commands apart.
6. Phone table length (phone-light-03 to -06): 14 cards × 5 rows is roughly four tall screens of near-identical cards. Let the reader pick a machine to compare against, or use a compact 5-column grid with the machine names abbreviated in a sticky header row (m5.l / c8i.2xl …). Then a benchmark takes about 2 rows of height instead of a 400 px card. At minimum, add a jump list of the five groups at the table's top.
7. Give units one form across the machine cards (desktop-light-01, The machines). Network reads 'Up to 10 Gigabit', 'Up to 15000 Megabit' and '12500 Megabit', and Processor ranges from 'Intel Xeon Platinum 8175' to 'AMD EPYC 9R45 Processor'. If these are AWS's own strings, say so in the section caption. Otherwise put every network figure in Gbps and drop the repeated 'Processor'. The cards are also tall for five facts each: they could be a compact five-column spec table that lines up with the headline table's columns, which already carry vCPU and price.
8. Clear up the gap between the run schedule and the clock (desktop-light-00, middle stat). Boots happen at 04:10/10:10/16:10/22:10, yet the 'newest Run' is 17:07. Add 'Runs follow each boot one after another' or show the boot time beside the newest Run. Also say what the dial is: it reads as a 24-hour dial only once you notice the '00' and '12' labels.

KEEP
- The hero's split: a plain claim headline on the left and 'One figure, traced to its source' on the right. The card carries the exact digits, a correctly scaled p5/p50/p95 bar, counted and failed Runs, the date span, the setting, the Method, the zone and price, and the Series URL. It is the best single statement of what the project is, and it reads well on phone and in dark mode.
- The 'Newest Run started…' line under the CTAs, and the footer's nanosecond snapshot timestamp.
- The dark agent section: curl plus Copy, a one-line 'what you get' under each command, schema links, and the real JSON excerpt of the very Series shown at the top, with the 'nothing rounded' caption. The excerpt closing the loop with the hero is excellent.
- The 'A Method, versioned and written down' section, which quotes the definitions (R type 7 and so on) verbatim. Rare, and right for this audience.
- Plain-English benchmark names with a one-sentence description, an explicit unit and a 'less/more is faster' cue. The column headers carry vCPU and $/h.
- The type system (serif display, sans body, mono for identifiers) and a warm palette whose dark mode is done properly rather than inverted.

FALSE, MISLEADING OR INVENTED
- 'Rounded to four significant figures' under a heading that says 'as measured', on a page whose JSON caption says 'nothing rounded'. See change 1.
- 'Random 4 KiB reads, 64 in flight' is described as 'How many direct reads the root EBS gp3 volume completes', which is a count or rate, but the figure is 'µs per repetition, less is faster'. Make the description and the unit agree. 'Sort 1 MiB… How fast one core copies and sorts' against a time unit is a milder version of the same slip.
- The identical Disk figures look like machine results but are the volume's limits (change 4).
- The mutex footnote ('the decimal point moved four places') is accurate but reads like an admission that the figure was edited. Define the unit instead: ns per critical section, from 10,000 per repetition.
- 'Hover a figure for its percentiles' appears on phone, where you cannot hover.
